extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers, aspiring essayists/writers, parents and those interested in manners, education, and taste
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive guidance for composing short moral/character essays and sketches (e.g., portraits of a 'Woman's Man', reflections on education, and definitions of 'genius'), including traits to depict, moral conclusions, and stylistic cautions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Woman's Man — appearance and manner
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'Woman's Man' is characterised by a loose, negligent garb and a soft, indolent manner; an apparent endeavour to appear unconcerned and careless. Signs include 'strutting': an elevated chest, a pinched hat, a measurable step, and a sly surveying eye.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These outward marks signal the character's role and social effect; any one of them can 'undo Thousands'. Use these visible traits in a sketch to indicate his profession of gallantry and to make the character recognisable to readers. The essay warns that such appearance often masks inconstancy and artifice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Woman's Man — conversational mimicry & practical attentions
rubrics_metrics.description: He imitates the female conversation he expects to encounter and keeps small officious attentions: knowing family gossip, offering remedies for a cold, and carrying a bottle of spirits for sudden indisposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray conversational mimicry and small ministrations to show how he ingratiates himself; these practical attentions are part of his calculated entertainment and social utility rather than signs of sincerity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Woman's Man — social strategy and reputation
rubrics_metrics.description: Success requires a reputation for being well with other women; inconstancy, a general fame for falsehood, and being 'loaded with the Favours of many others' often increase his appeal. He keeps women from explaining matters to each other and profits from rivalry among them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When creating such a figure, emphasise reputation and social manoeuvres — not true attachment — as the source of his success. The text treats inconstancy and artful reputation as assets rather than vices in this social economy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Woman's Man — types: regular visitants vs 'ruiners' of ladies
rubrics_metrics.description: Several species: 'regular Visitants' (volunteers who lead ladies out from public places, admitted on public days) and 'Ruiners of Ladies' (accomplished fellows with knowledge of Court and Town, publicly decent but privately dissolute).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these typologies to vary scenes and social roles: regulars provide harmless company, ruiners are the accomplished, dangerous charmers. The distinction helps dramatise differing moral consequences and social expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entertaining is better than sensible for success with women
rubrics_metrics.description: To be a successful 'Woman's Man' one need 'not be a Man of Sense, or a Fool'; 'the Business is to entertain, and it is much better to have a Faculty of arguing, than a Capacity of judging right.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In character construction, prioritise wit, argument, and entertaining manners over sound judgement. The point is prescriptive about what the fair sex rewards, and thus how a portrait should be written for verisimilitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Female taste: affectation and trivial excellencies over solid virtues
rubrics_metrics.description: Women in the described circle 'are got into a Way of Affectation, with a manner of overlooking the most solid Virtues, and admiring the most trivial Excellencies.' They value features and mien and cultivate 'amiable in Imperfection.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When depicting social interactions, foreground how flattery, fashion, and small graces outweigh deeper qualities. This explains motivations and social dynamics in portraits and moral essays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider natural disposition (indoles) in education
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'natural Disposition to any Particular Art, Science, Profession, or Trade' must be consulted in the care of youth; schoolmasters should discern capacities and not force the same course on all children.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a prescriptive standard for education, insist that tutors and parents observe individual talents and fit instruction to them; use concrete examples (children unsuited to classical learning) to justify divergent paths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid corporal punishment; preserve conscience and virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: Punishing by the lash is destructive: it 'brings [a child] below the Existence of a rational Creature' and spoils good minds. The sense of shame and honour should govern behaviour rather than corporal punishment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argue against harsh disciplinary methods; portray punishment as counterproductive to the cultivation of virtue and learning. Use emotive examples (a child kneeling in tears) to dramatise the harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Early vocational sorting based on capacity, not birth
rubrics_metrics.description: Children should be examined early; those unsuited to letters should be 'sent to some Mechanick Way of Life, without respect to his Birth' rather than be kept in school and debased by punishment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advocate practical assessment and timely redirection of youths into trades when natural capacity indicates. This is a procedural recommendation with moral and social justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach by allurement and encouragement, not by blows
rubrics_metrics.description: No boy who will not be allured to letters without blows will be brought to anything by them; great minds are made worse by indignities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In educational practice and in rhetorical argument about education, favour incentives, honour, and encouragement as more effective means of forming intellect and character than coercion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Life allegory — life as a bridge with hidden pitfalls
rubrics_metrics.description: Human life is represented as a bridge across Time with many trap-doors at the entrances (early life) and fewer in the middle; many passengers are distracted by 'Bubbles' and fall unexpectedly. Vices and passions (Vultures, Harpies, Ravens, Cormorants; Envy, Avarice, Superstition, Despair, Love) hover above and push people into pitfalls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this allegory in moral writing to visualise human frailty: show how distraction and particular vices produce sudden moral or literal falls. The concrete images (trap-doors, birds, bubbles) function as cautionary devices to instruct readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtue as means to an ordered afterlife reward
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond the bridge is an ocean with innumerable islands — 'Mansions of good Men' — distributed 'according to the Degree and Kinds of Virtue' in life; these islands offer pleasures suited to the inhabitants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame moral argument around the proportionality of reward: cultivate different kinds and degrees of virtue to attain corresponding felicities. This provides teleological motivation in didactic writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a great genius — natural, untrained force
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'great Genius' is one who, by the mere strength of 'natural Parts' and 'without any Assistance of Arts or Learning,' produces works of wonder; such genius is 'nobly wild and extravagant.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When characterising extraordinary creativity, emphasize spontaneous force and originality, the kind of unchecked imagination exemplified by figures like Homer and Shakespeare.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bel Esprit/refined genius — polish by art and reading
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'Bel Esprit' is a genius refined by conversation, reflection, and reading of polite authors; this refinement produces nicety, correctness, and decorum ('bienséance').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between raw imaginative power and cultivated elegance. In stylistic advice, encourage study and polish for writers who aim at correctness and precise allusion rather than unbridled sublimity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not imitate natural irregularity by rule
rubrics_metrics.description: It is ridiculous for sober and moderate fancies to imitate the irregularities of poets like Pindar by rule; following 'Irregularities by Rule' or 'straining after the most unbounded Flights of Nature' is absurd.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warn writers against mechanical imitation of grand irregular styles; irregularity must be genuine, not a trick of artifice. This is both a stylistic anti-pattern and a practical guideline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of decorum and nicety in modern composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern writers should observe nicety and exactness (the French _bienséance_) in allusion and comparison; the ancients' force does not excuse indecency of comparison.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promote decorum and tasteful allusion in contemporary writing: prefer precise, decent comparisons rather than the grand but sometimes indecent similitudes of earlier poets.
